content: Female fertility refers to a woman's natural ability to conceive and bear children. It depends on multiple physiological mechanisms, including ovulation (the release of a mature egg from the ovaries), hormonal regulation by the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis, and a healthy reproductive tract to support fertilization and implantation. Synonyms and related terms include reproductive potential, fecundity, and ovarian reserve. Female fertility naturally declines with age, notably after the mid-30s, due to decreasing quantity and quality of ovarian follicles. Various factors influence fertility such as genetics, lifestyle, environmental exposures, and medical conditions like polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) or endometriosis. Practical relevance for consumers includes understanding ovulation timing, recognizing when to seek fertility evaluation, and awareness of fertility preservation options. Limitations exist regarding the predictability of fertility based solely on age or single tests, as well as the efficacy and accessibility of treatments. Safety considerations include risks associated with fertility medications, procedures like in vitro fertilization (IVF), and potential impacts on maternal and offspring health. Understanding normal physiology and common interventions empowers informed decisions but requires consultation with healthcare professionals for personalized guidance.

content: Fundamental physiological processes that support female fertility include the menstrual cycle, dominated by the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis. The cycle regulates follicular development, ovulation, and preparation of the endometrial lining for implantation. Key hormones include follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), luteinizing hormone (LH), estrogen, and progesterone. Disruptions in this axis can impair fertility.

chunk_title: Role of the Menstrual Cycle in Fertility
content: The menstrual cycle typically lasts 28 ± 7 days, with ovulation occurring mid-cycle. Fertility peaks during the ovulatory window when a mature egg is available for fertilization, typically the 5 days leading up to and including ovulation. Understanding cycle phases helps in timing intercourse or treatments to improve chances of conception.

content: Female fertility naturally declines with age, especially after age 35. This decline results from reduced ovarian reserve (the number of viable eggs) and lower egg quality, increasing risks of infertility and miscarriage. Menopause marks the end of natural fertility. Age-related decline varies individually but influences family planning decisions.

content: Several factors impact female fertility including lifestyle elements like smoking, alcohol intake, body weight extremes, and stress. Medical conditions such as polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), endometriosis, thyroid disorders, and pelvic inflammatory disease can impair fertility. Environmental exposures and genetic factors also contribute.

content: Fertility assessment includes history taking, physical examination, and diagnostic tests. Common tests include hormone assays (FSH, LH, estradiol, anti-Müllerian hormone/AMH), ultrasound evaluation of antral follicle count, and imaging of reproductive organs. These assess ovarian reserve, ovulation status, and structural factors relevant to fertility potential.
